actions.name: Review colonoscopy procedure note
actions.result: Colonoscopy to cecum, good prep. Single 14 mm pedunculated polyp identified in sigmoid colon, removed intact by snare polypectomy (en bloc). Base/stalk tattooed for localization. No other polyps or masses seen. Retrieved specimen sent whole to pathology.

actions.name: Review surgical pathology report (final)
actions.result: Specimen: sigmoid colon polypectomy, 14 mm, pedunculated, submitted in toto (whole specimen). Diagnosis: Tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia. Stalk (resection) margin negative for dysplasia. No invasive carcinoma identified. Representative sections examined; entire polyp processed.

actions.name: Confirm complete submission of specimen (gross exam notes)
actions.result: Gross description confirms polyp was received intact, measured, inked at stalk margin, and entirely submitted for microscopic sectioning (no residual tissue retained in block for further sampling).

actions.name: Review family history documentation in chart
actions.result: Problem list and intake note: brother diagnosed with 'colon polyps' at approximately age 43-45; no documented genetic syndrome, no known Lynch syndrome or FAP diagnosis in family.

actions.name: Review immunohistochemistry / special stains status
actions.result: No immunohistochemical or molecular studies were performed or needed; diagnosis made on routine H&E morphology alone. Mismatch repair (MMR) protein stains were not ordered because this adenoma does not meet criteria for universal screening (that applies to colorectal carcinoma, not adenomas).

actions.name: Review prior biopsy or pathology history
actions.result: No prior colonoscopy or pathology specimens on file for this patient; this is her first colonoscopy and first polyp removed.

actions.name: Check polyp size/morphology measurement documentation
actions.result: Gross measurement confirms 14 mm greatest dimension, pedunculated (on a stalk) morphology, consistent with endoscopic description.

actions.name: Review complete blood count (unrelated screening)
actions.result: Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL (ref 12.0-15.5), WBC 6.8 x10^9/L (ref 4.0-11.0), platelets 245 x10^9/L (ref 150-400). No anemia.

actions.name: Review gastroenterology follow-up plan in chart
actions.result: GI note indicates follow-up appointment scheduled in 3 weeks to discuss results and plan next surveillance colonoscopy interval; no interim action required.

artifacts.title: Colonoscopy Procedure Note
artifacts.author: Dr. Patel, Gastroenterology
artifacts.body:
PROCEDURE: Colonoscopy with polypectomy
INDICATION: Positive fecal immunochemical test (FIT), average-risk screening
FINDINGS: Scope advanced to cecum; good bowel preparation; a single 14 mm pedunculated polyp identified in the sigmoid colon. Polyp removed in one piece using hot snare polypectomy. Base of stalk marked with India ink tattoo for future localization. No other polyps, masses, or abnormal mucosa identified throughout the colon. Specimen retrieved intact and sent to pathology in a single container.
IMPRESSION: Single sigmoid polyp, completely excised.
PLAN: Await pathology; routine post-polypectomy follow-up.

artifacts.title: Surgical Pathology Report
artifacts.author: Dept. of Pathology

cells: Tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia
Dysplasia involves a small focal area within the adenoma
No invasion through muscularis mucosae seen in any section
All tissue examined microscopically, nothing withheld

artifacts.body: FINAL DIAGNOSIS: Sigmoid colon, polypectomy: Tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia. Stalk margin negative for dysplasia. No invasive carcinoma identified. COMMENT: The entire polyp was processed and examined. The area of high-grade dysplasia is confined to the adenoma and does not extend to or involve the resection margin.

artifacts.title: Gastroenterology Clinic Note (prior visit)
artifacts.author: Dr. Patel, Gastroenterology
artifacts.body: 44-year-old woman referred for colonoscopy after positive FIT screening test. No GI symptoms, no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habits. Family history notable for a brother with colon polyps diagnosed in his early 40s; no known hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome in the family. Plan: colonoscopy with polypectomy as indicated; follow-up visit scheduled 3 weeks after procedure to review pathology and establish surveillance interval.

facts.chart: Patient requests explanation of colon polyp pathology report before scheduled GI follow-up; concerned the report means she has cancer
facts.says: I got my results on the patient portal and it says 'high-grade dysplasia' and I looked it up and I think that means I have cancer. My doctor's appointment isn't for three more weeks and I can't wait that long not knowing.

facts.chart: Polyp found on first colonoscopy, prompted by positive stool screening test (FIT)
facts.says: I'd never had a colonoscopy before. I did one of those at-home stool tests my doctor sent me, and it came back positive, so they said I needed the scope.

facts.chart: No GI symptoms prior to screening; asymptomatic average-risk screening detection
facts.says: I didn't have any symptoms at all. No blood, no pain, nothing. That's part of why this is so scary - I felt completely fine.

facts.chart: Single polyp removed during colonoscopy via snare polypectomy, patient recalls doctor saying it was removed completely
facts.says: The doctor told me right after that they got the whole thing out in one piece and it looked like just a growth, not anything scary, but then I read the report and panicked.

facts.chart: Patient interprets 'high-grade dysplasia' as synonymous with invasive cancer based on internet search
facts.says: I googled it and some website said high-grade dysplasia can turn into cancer, and I just assumed that meant I already have it.

facts.chart: Brother diagnosed with colon polyps in his early-to-mid 40s; no known hereditary syndrome diagnosed in family
facts.says: My brother had polyps too, found when he was like 43 or 44. Nobody in my family's ever been told they have one of those genetic colon cancer syndromes though, if that's what you're asking.

facts.chart: No other first-degree relatives with colorectal or related cancers reported
facts.says: My parents are both healthy, no colon cancer that I know of. No other brothers or sisters.

facts.chart: Denies rectal bleeding, melena, or hematochezia currently or before procedure
facts.says: No, I've never seen blood in the toilet or anything like that.

facts.chart: Denies recent change in bowel habits, diarrhea, or constipation
facts.says: My bathroom habits have been pretty normal, no changes I've noticed.

facts.chart: Denies unintentional weight loss
facts.says: My weight's been steady, nothing unusual there.

facts.chart: Denies abdominal pain
facts.says: No stomach pain or cramping, I feel fine physically.

facts.chart: Patient reports significant anxiety and difficulty sleeping since reading the pathology report online
facts.says: Honestly I haven't slept well the past week. I keep rereading the report at 2am trying to figure out what it means.

facts.chart: Patient's primary fear is that 'high-grade dysplasia' equals cancer that was missed or left behind
facts.says: What I really want to know is - did they get all of it? Is there cancer still in me that they didn't take out?

facts.chart: Patient specifically requested to speak with pathology rather than wait for GI, stating she wanted the person who actually looked at the tissue
facts.says: I asked specifically to talk to whoever looked at it under the microscope, because I want to hear it straight from the source, not secondhand.

facts.chart: Colonoscopy performed 2 weeks ago; pathology report posted to portal 10 days ago; GI follow-up scheduled 3 weeks from today
facts.says: The procedure was two weeks ago, I saw the report pop up on the portal about ten days ago, and my follow-up with the GI doctor isn't for another three weeks.

facts.chart: Patient asks why she would need another colonoscopy in three years if the polyp was already removed
facts.says: If they already took it out, why would I need another colonoscopy in three years? Doesn't that seem too soon, or does that mean they think there's more?

facts.chart: Patient unfamiliar with meaning of 'margin negative' and asks for clarification
facts.says: What does 'margin negative' even mean? Is that good news or bad news?

facts.chart: Former smoker, quit 8 years ago, previously 5 pack-years
facts.says: I used to smoke in my twenties, maybe half a pack a day for about ten years, but I quit eight years ago.

facts.chart: Reports diet moderate in red meat, tries to eat vegetables most days
facts.says: I probably eat red meat a couple times a week, and I try to get vegetables in most days, but I work a desk job so I'm not always great about it.

facts.chart: Patient works as hospital billing specialist; has taken no time off work due to this issue but reports distraction at work from worry
facts.says: I work in medical billing actually, so I know how to read some of this stuff, but this report still threw me. I've been distracted at work worrying about it.

facts.chart: Patient does not know baseline meaning of 'adenoma' versus cancer
facts.says: Is an adenoma a type of cancer, or is that something else? I honestly don't know what that word means.

facts.chart: Patient worried the same polyp could grow back in the same spot
facts.says: Can this exact same polyp come back where they cut it out, like regrow?

facts.chart: Patient asks whether she or her brother should get genetic testing for colon cancer syndromes
facts.says: Should my brother and I get some kind of genetic test, since we both had polyps around the same age?

facts.chart: Patient expresses some frustration that GI team did not explain findings in more detail before the scheduled follow-up
facts.says: I just feel like someone should have called me sooner to explain this instead of leaving me to google it myself for ten days.

facts.chart: Patient asks whether more tissue testing (genetic/molecular) is needed on the polyp itself
facts.says: Do they need to run more tests on the piece they took out, like genetic testing on the tissue itself?

facts.chart: Patient works in billing and is concerned about cost of additional procedures or tests
facts.says: Working in billing, I can't help but think about costs too - is a repeat colonoscopy going to be covered, or is this going to be a fight with insurance?

facts.chart: Patient does not understand what 'pedunculated' means in the report
facts.says: It also says the polyp was 'pedunculated' - what does that mean exactly?

facts.topic: question about why no chemo or further treatment
facts.chart: Patient surprised that no additional cancer treatment (chemo, surgery) was recommended and wonders if that was an oversight
facts.says: If there's dysplasia, shouldn't I be getting chemotherapy or more surgery? Nobody's mentioned any of that and it's making me more nervous, not less.

facts.topic: what patient wants from this visit
facts.chart: Patient's stated goal for the consult is a clear, plain-language explanation of whether cancer is present and what the follow-up plan means
facts.says: I just want someone to tell me plainly - cancer or not, and what happens next - in words I can actually understand.

facts.chart: No significant past medical history; no prior cancer diagnosis
facts.says: I don't really have any other health problems. This is honestly the first scary medical thing that's happened to me.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient recalls the endoscopist saying the polyp was removed completely and 'looked like just a growth, not anything scary' right after the procedure
mismatches.recordEvidence: The procedure note documents complete removal in one piece but does not characterize the polyp's appearance as benign-looking; it simply states findings and awaits pathology, since gross appearance alone cannot determine dysplasia grade
mismatches.teachingPoint: Visual impression during endoscopy cannot predict microscopic dysplasia grade; reassurance given at the time of the procedure should be understood as provisional, pending the final pathology report, not a final determination.

objectives.text: Accurately explain the specimen, diagnosis, and terminology (tubular adenoma, high-grade dysplasia, pedunculated, margin status) in plain language appropriate to the patient's health literacy
Correctly distinguish high-grade dysplasia from invasive carcinoma and clarify that no cancer was found, directly addressing the patient's core fear

Explain what is known (complete excision, clear margin) versus what remains uncertain or outside pathology's determination (future risk, management decisions) and appropriately hand back to gastroenterology for surveillance planning

Elicit and appropriately contextualize family history, recognizing that a brother with polyps at a similar age raises surveillance considerations without overstating genetic risk or ordering testing outside scope

Identify and gently address the mismatch between the patient's recollection of reassuring verbal comments at the time of procedure and the more neutral/provisional documentation, modeling clear risk communication

Recognize the emotional impact of ambiguous pathology terminology and respond with empathy while staying within the pathology consultant's scope (no treatment recommendations, refer management questions to gastroenterology)

patient.name: Renee Okafor
patient.appearance: A woman in her mid-40s with short natural hair, wearing a cardigan over a blouse, seated at a tidy home desk with a laptop and a notebook open beside her. Her posture is upright and alert, with a furrowed brow and the practiced focus of someone who has clearly reread a document many times before this call.

persona.personality: Analytical, detail-oriented, and assertive; wants precise information and notices hedging or vague language immediately
persona.communicationStyle: Direct, asks pointed follow-up questions, often references specific words from the report, appreciates when answers are concrete
persona.emotionalState: Anxious but composed; working to control the anxiety through information-seeking rather than panic
persona.background: Born in the UK to Nigerian parents, moved to the US in her twenties, now works in hospital billing in Atlanta where she has become familiar with medical terminology and documentation from her job, though not clinical pathology; enjoys gardening on weekends and is close with her brother who lives nearby.
speechExamples: It says right here 'focal high-grade dysplasia' - focal meaning what, exactly, just one spot?
I work in billing, so I'm used to reading medical documents, but this is a different language entirely.
Can you point to exactly where it says that in the report, because I don't see it.
I don't want the version that makes me feel better, I want the version that's true.
concerns: Whether any cancerous tissue was left behind in her body
Why a 3-year follow-up colonoscopy would be recommended if the polyp is already gone
Whether her brother's polyp history means they both need genetic testing
Why no additional cancer treatment (chemotherapy, surgery) has been recommended

scenario.studentBrief: You are a pathology resident holding a patient-requested telehealth consultation. Renee Okafor, 44, had her first colonoscopy after a positive stool screening test, during which a 14 mm polyp was removed. She found her pathology report on the patient portal and requested to speak with pathology directly because her gastroenterology follow-up is three weeks away. Your task is to explain the specimen and diagnosis in plain language, clarify what is and is not known, and hand back management decisions to her gastroenterologist.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Patient-requested explanation of colon polyp pathology report; fears the report means she has cancer
scenario.openingLine: Thank you for seeing me on such short notice. I got my pathology results on the portal and it says I have 'high-grade dysplasia,' and from what I've read online, I'm worried that means I have cancer. My gastroenterologist appointment isn't for three more weeks and I couldn't just sit with this.
tasks: Explain in plain language what tissue was examined and what the pathology terms in the report mean
Clearly state what is known from the pathology examination and what remains outside pathology's determination (such as surveillance interval or need for additional procedures)
Address the patient's concerns and questions about the findings
Discuss any relevant family history without overstepping into ordering tests or making management recommendations
Appropriately hand back decisions about surveillance timing and any further referrals to her gastroenterologist

answerKey.primaryProblem: Tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia, completely excised with negative margin, no invasive carcinoma - a precancerous (not cancerous) lesion that was fully removed
differential: Tubular adenoma with high-grade dysplasia (confirmed diagnosis)
Invasive adenocarcinoma arising in adenoma (explicitly excluded by pathology)
Hyperplastic/sessile serrated polyp (not applicable; morphology was adenomatous)
Hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome (e.g., Lynch syndrome) given brother's early polyp - not diagnosed, warrants discussion with GI/genetics but not determined by this specimen
keyFindings: 14 mm pedunculated sigmoid polyp removed completely in one piece (en bloc)
Final diagnosis: tubular adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia
Stalk/resection margin negative for dysplasia - clear margin
No invasive carcinoma identified; dysplasia confined within the adenoma, has not breached into the deeper bowel wall
Entire polyp was submitted and examined microscopically - no untested tissue remains in the specimen
Family history: brother with colon polyps in early-to-mid 40s; no known hereditary syndrome diagnosed in family
plan: Reassure patient that no cancer was found and the premalignant tissue was completely removed with a clear margin
Explain that high-grade dysplasia is a severity grade within the adenoma itself, not evidence of invasive cancer, and does not require chemotherapy or additional surgery

Clarify that pathology's role is limited to describing the specimen; decisions about surveillance colonoscopy timing are made by the gastroenterologist based on the full clinical picture, including society guidelines - this determination is outside the pathology consult's scope and should be deferred to GI

Note that family history of early-onset polyps is relevant and should be discussed with gastroenterology, who may consider referral to genetic counseling or earlier surveillance for her and her brother; pathology does not order or interpret germline genetic testing
Document the consult and communicate directly with the gastroenterology team so the discussion is available before the scheduled follow-up visit
Encourage patient to bring her remaining questions about surveillance interval and genetic testing to the already-scheduled GI follow-up
redFlags: Any indication of invasive carcinoma on re-review (not present here - margin clear, no invasion identified)
Incomplete polyp excision or inability to assess margin (not applicable - polyp was removed intact and entirely submitted)

Multiple relatives with early-onset colorectal cancer or polyps suggesting hereditary syndrome requiring urgent genetics referral (current history shows one brother with polyps, not yet meeting criteria for urgent syndrome workup, but worth flagging to GI)
educationPoints: 'High-grade dysplasia' describes the most severe degree of precancerous cellular change within a polyp - it means the cells look very abnormal under the microscope, but it is not the same as invasive cancer, which requires breach of the muscularis mucosae
'Tubular adenoma' names the growth pattern of this common type of precancerous colon polyp
'Pedunculated' simply describes the polyp's shape - on a stalk, like a mushroom - which often makes complete snare removal easier
A negative margin means the plane where the polyp was cut away from the bowel wall shows no dysplastic cells, supporting that the entire abnormal area was removed

Routine surveillance colonoscopy is a precaution to check for new polyps, not evidence that something was missed or left behind; the specific interval is a gastroenterology management decision outside the pathology consult's scope
Pathology confirms what was found in the tissue sample; recommendations about future procedures, timing, and genetic counselling referrals belong to the treating gastroenterologist

profile.title: Explaining 'High-Grade Dysplasia': A Patient-Requested Pathology Consult After Polypectomy
profile.summary: A 44-year-old billing specialist who had her first colonoscopy after a positive stool screening test requests a pathology consultation to understand her polyp report before her gastroenterology follow-up in three weeks. The case teaches learners to translate pathology terminology (tubular adenoma, high-grade dysplasia, margin status) into plain language, distinguish dysplasia from invasive cancer, and appropriately defer management and surveillance-interval decisions to the gastroenterology team.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home desk in Atlanta, Georgia
